strengths: Novel and creative idea: repurposing TabPFN, a tabular in-context-learning foundation model, as a gradient-free Q-function approximator within a Fitted Q Iteration framework, avoiding backpropagation entirely at both training and inference.

The paper provides an honest theoretical discussion of why TabPFN's i.i.d. task-prior assumptions are violated by bootstrapped Bellman targets and non-stationary visitation distributions, which is a useful conceptual framing even if informal.

Explicitly identifies and addresses the context-budget limitation shared by all in-context-learning RL methods, proposing and empirically comparing four concrete truncation heuristics (Latest, Naive De-duplication, Embedding De-duplication, Reward Variance) against sensible baselines (stale context, latest-B).
Reasonably detailed implementation appendix (library versions, hyperparameters, reward-shaping formulas, hardware) supports partial reproducibility.
Includes an ablation study over key hyperparameters (percentile refit threshold, epsilon decay, initial epsilon, context budget size) with multiple seeds.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to three very simple, low-dimensional classic-control tasks with small discrete action spaces (CartPole, MountainCar, Acrobot); no evidence is given that the approach scales beyond toy settings, which substantially limits the significance of the claimed contribution.

All three environments require hand-crafted reward shaping for TabPFN-RL to work well, and the paper explicitly states the method struggles with sparse rewards without further analysis; this undercuts the central claim of general applicability and makes the DQN comparison less informative about real-world efficacy.

The DQN baseline's tuning quality is unclear (e.g., infrequent target-network updates for only 250 training episodes), and no comparison to other in-context/meta-RL baselines (RL2, Algorithm Distillation, OmniRL) is provided empirically despite being discussed at length in related work, leaving the competitiveness claim only partially substantiated.

The 'theoretical' contributions (task-prior mismatch, context-size limitation) are largely descriptive/qualitative rather than formalized with proofs, bounds, or quantitative predictions that are then verified.

The context-truncation ablation (Figure 2) is only conducted on a single environment (MountainCar-v0), so it is unclear whether the reported superiority of Naive De-duplication generalizes to other tasks or action/state spaces.

Computational cost claims (quadratic inference scaling with context size) are discussed but not empirically quantified in wall-clock time or FLOPs, despite this being a key practical trade-off for the proposed method (context budgets up to 8192 are used in ablations).
No code release is mentioned, and given the many moving parts (context management, refit triggers, truncation heuristics), independent reproduction would be nontrivial from the paper text alone.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are shown as mean±band curves without explicit significance testing, and the number of seeds (10 for main comparison, 5 for ablations) is modest for environments with known high variance (e.g., CartPole, MountainCar).

strengths: The core idea of repurposing TabPFN, a prior-fitted transformer trained for tabular ICL, as a drop-in Q-function approximator inside Fitted Q Iteration is creative and underexplored, and it is a reasonable extension of the growing literature on ICL for RL.

The paper is transparent about a genuine and interesting theoretical tension: TabPFN's meta-training prior assumes i.i.d. rows, whereas FQI targets are bootstrapped and non-stationary. Explicitly surfacing this mismatch and still finding the model works is a worthwhile observation for the community.

The context-budget problem for in-context RL methods (what to do once the context window is full) is a real and largely unaddressed issue, and the paper proposes several concrete truncation heuristics (Latest, Naive/Embedding De-duplication, Reward Variance) with an empirical comparison.
Reasonably detailed appendix with hyperparameters, reward-shaping formulas, and hardware specification, which aids partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to three low-dimensional, classic-control Gymnasium tasks (CartPole, MountainCar, Acrobot) with heavy, hand-crafted, per-environment reward shaping. This severely limits the significance of the claimed contribution; the paper itself admits it does not know how the method behaves in sparse-reward or high-dimensional settings, which are exactly the regimes where gradient-free/ICL RL would be most valuable.

The abstract and discussion claim TabPFN-RL 'matches or surpasses DQN' with 'no extensive hyperparameter tuning,' but Figure 1 shows DQN reaching a substantially better asymptotic reward on Acrobot-v1, and the ablation study (Figure 3) shows strong sensitivity to percentile refit threshold, epsilon schedule, initial epsilon, and context budget B — directly contradicting the 'no extensive tuning' framing and the 'matches or surpasses' claim.

A central selling point is computational/gradient-free efficiency, yet the paper explicitly acknowledges that TabPFN inference cost grows quadratically with context size and 'can outweigh the savings from omitting back-propagation,' but no wall-clock time, FLOPs, or memory comparison against DQN is ever reported, leaving the efficiency claim unsubstantiated.

The 'theoretical' sections (Task-Prior Mismatch, Theoretical Limitations of ICL RL) are largely qualitative/narrative rather than formal: there are no theorems, bounds, or quantitative predictions that are subsequently tested, despite being framed as a principled contribution ('we formalize the intrinsic context size limit').

DQN baseline details are thin (no architecture description, e.g., hidden layer sizes) and no other relevant gradient-free baselines (evolution strategies, KNN-TD, PPO) are empirically compared, despite being discussed at length in related work; this makes it hard to judge whether TabPFN-RL's advantage over 'RL with gradients' is real or an artifact of a weak/undertuned baseline.

Only 250 training episodes per environment and 10 seeds are used; no statistical significance testing is reported, and shaded regions in figures are not clearly defined (std vs. CI), weakening the strength of the empirical claims.

No code release is mentioned, and the described hyperparameters (e.g., percentile refit, iteration counts) are not exhaustively specified for the context-truncation experiments, limiting reproducibility of the continual-learning results in Figure 2.

The contribution is primarily an empirical repurposing of an existing pretrained model on toy benchmarks rather than a new algorithmic or theoretical advance, and given the narrow evaluation and overclaiming relative to the actual results, the overall significance for the broader RL community is limited.

strengths: The core idea is novel: repurposing TabPFN, a prior-fitted transformer trained for tabular ICL, as a Q-function approximator inside a Fitted-Q-Iteration loop, entirely avoiding backpropagation at both training and inference. This is an interesting and previously unexplored application of prior-fitted networks to RL.

The paper explicitly and honestly discusses the theoretical tension between TabPFN's i.i.d. meta-training prior and the bootstrapped, non-stationary, sequentially-correlated data encountered in RL, which is a useful conceptual framing for the community even if not formally proven.

The proposed context-truncation heuristics (Latest, Naive/Embedding De-duplication, Reward-Variance) address a genuine and under-explored problem for all in-context RL methods -- what to do once the fixed context budget is exhausted -- and the empirical comparison (Fig. 2) shows a sensible ordering of methods.
The appendix provides fairly detailed implementation information (library versions, hyperparameters, reward-shaping formulas, hardware), which aids reproducibility.

Limitations (need for reward shaping, quadratic inference cost with context size, hyperparameter sensitivity, unclear scaling to high-dimensional/sparse-reward tasks) are discussed candidly rather than hidden.
weaknesses: Empirical validation is narrow: only three low-dimensional Gymnasium classic-control tasks are used, and even there results are mixed -- e.g., in the Acrobot-v1 plot DQN appears to converge to a clearly better (higher) return than TabPFN-RL, which is at odds with the abstract's claim that the method 'matches or surpasses DQN' on all three environments.

All three environments required custom, environment-specific reward shaping for TabPFN-RL to work well, which undercuts the practical appeal of a 'no extensive hyperparameter tuning' gradient-free method and raises unresolved questions about applicability to naturally sparse-reward tasks.

The claimed theoretical contributions ('we formalize the intrinsic context size limit,' 'theoretical aspects of prior mismatch') are largely narrative/qualitative arguments rather than formal results (no theorems, bounds, or proofs), so the paper's framing overstates the rigor of this contribution.

The hyperparameter ablations (percentile refit, epsilon decay, initial epsilon, context budget B) are conducted on a single environment (MountainCar-v0) with only 5 seeds, limiting confidence that the selected settings generalize to other tasks; similarly, the context-truncation comparison in Fig. 2 is on one environment.

The DQN baseline uses a single fixed hyperparameter configuration with no indication of tuning effort, whereas the paper stresses DQN's hyperparameter sensitivity; without comparable tuning budgets for both methods, the head-to-head comparison is not fully controlled.

Computational/wall-clock cost of TabPFN-RL versus DQN is not reported, despite the paper itself noting that inference scales quadratically with context size; without runtime numbers, the practical trade-off between avoiding backprop and paying for large-context transformer inference cannot be assessed.

No code repository link is provided, and given the many implementation-specific choices (episode capping length L, exact context construction, noise injection before FQI, gate quantile), independent reproduction would be difficult without released code.

The related-work/method framing does not empirically compare against other gradient-free baselines mentioned in the introduction (Evolution Strategies, KNN-TD) or against PPO, despite these being discussed at length; the empirical comparison is limited solely to DQN.

strengths: The core idea—reducing RL to in-context regression via a classical FQI reduction and instantiating it with an off-the-shelf regression foundation model (TabPFN) with zero RL-specific training—is a genuinely interesting and reasonably original angle on gradient-free RL and foundation models for control.

The paper is generally clearly written, with a well-organized related-work section that carefully differentiates the proposed approach from Decision/Trajectory Transformer, RL2, Algorithm Distillation, ICQL, BFMs, and OmniRL along concrete axes (gradient-free, zero-shot, RL-pretraining-free, continuous-state support), summarized helpfully in Table 1.

The context-engineering study (naive/embedding de-duplication, reward-variance retention, stale/latest-episode baselines) is a useful, self-contained contribution addressing a practical bottleneck (fixed context budget under quadratic attention cost) that is under-addressed in prior in-context RL work.

The authors include a reasonably extensive set of ablations (FQI iteration count via alpha, epsilon-schedule, context budget, percentile refit threshold) and additional baselines (KNN-based FQI, TabICL, TabFlex) in the appendix, adding some robustness to the empirical claims.

The discussion section honestly engages with why the approach should not work in principle (i.i.d. violation, non-stationary bootstrapped targets, distribution shift) which is a thoughtful and appropriately self-critical framing rather than glossing over the mismatch.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to three very simple, low-dimensional classic-control tasks (CartPole, MountainCar, Acrobot) run for only 250 episodes; there is no evidence the method scales beyond toy problems, and the authors themselves acknowledge this is untested, which substantially limits the significance of the claimed contribution.

The method requires environment-specific dense reward shaping for every task (Appendix B.2) because it 'tends not to perform well with sparse rewards.' This undercuts a central motivating claim of the paper (removing brittle, hand-tuned components of deep RL), since manually engineering a bespoke shaped reward per environment is itself a form of task-specific tuning/domain knowledge, arguably worse than tuning a few RL hyperparameters.

The paper repeatedly claims ICR-RL avoids the hyperparameter sensitivity of PPO/TRPO/DQN, yet the appendix ablations (alpha/iteration count, epsilon0, lambda decay, context budget B, percentile refit threshold) show substantial sensitivity to several ICR-RL-specific hyperparameters, undermining this claimed advantage.

No wall-clock or compute comparison is provided against DQN/PPO/TRPO baselines, despite the paper's own emphasis on the quadratic cost of transformer inference and repeated ICR-FQI refits over a growing context; only relative runtime across context-engineering variants is shown (Fig. 5), leaving the practical cost/benefit of the whole approach unclear.

The baseline RL algorithms appear notably underperforming relative to typical published results on these very simple benchmarks within the given episode budget (e.g., PPO barely reaching ~100 reward on CartPole after 250 episodes, TRPO struggling similarly), raising concern about whether baselines were adequately tuned/matched in sample budget, which could bias the comparison in ICR-RL's favor.

Episodes are not a compute- or sample-normalized unit across algorithms with different rollout/update structures (e.g., PPO's on-policy horizon of 2048 steps vs. per-step online updates in ICR-RL), making the episode-based comparison in Figure 2 potentially misleading as a measure of relative sample efficiency.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are shown with shaded bands that visibly overlap across methods in several plots, without significance testing, and the number of seeds (10) is modest for the variance observed.
It is unclear on which environment(s) the context-engineering experiments (Figures 3-5) were run, and this is not clearly stated in the main text, limiting reproducibility of a key set of claims.

The theoretical justification for why an i.i.d.-trained regression prior should work well under FQI's non-stationary, correlated, bootstrapped targets is largely qualitative/post-hoc rather than analytically grounded, leaving the central empirical puzzle (why it works) unresolved beyond speculation.

Minor issues: duplicate references ([32] and [33] are the same TabFlex paper), and some claims (e.g., 'continuous state-action spaces' support) are not directly tested with a continuous-action environment in the experiments.

strengths: The core idea—reducing RL to in-context regression via FQI and leveraging an off-the-shelf tabular foundation model (TabPFN) with no gradient-based training—is conceptually interesting and a reasonable instantiation of a classical reduction.
The paper is generally clearly written, with a well-structured method section (ICR-FQI vs ICR-RL distinction) and clear algorithmic pseudocode.

A reasonably thorough set of ablations is attempted (context engineering strategies, context budget size, epsilon-schedule, FQI iteration count, alternative ICR backbones such as TabICL/TabFlex), showing some effort toward understanding sensitivity to hyperparameters.

The related work section situates the contribution relative to decision transformers, trajectory transformers, RL^2, Algorithm Distillation, ICQL, and OmniRL reasonably well, clarifying what is genuinely novel (no RL-specific pretraining, zero-shot generalization).
weaknesses: Extremely limited empirical scope: only three classic-control Gymnasium environments (CartPole, MountainCar, Acrobot), all low-dimensional and relatively easy. No evidence the method scales beyond toy control, which severely limits the significance of the claimed contribution to a general 'foundation model for RL' paradigm.

Heavy reliance on hand-crafted, per-environment dense reward shaping (detailed in Appendix B.2) undermines the core selling point of a general-purpose, pretraining-free RL solution; the authors themselves acknowledge the method fails under sparse rewards without this shaping, which is a major undisclosed-until-appendix caveat relative to the strong claims in the abstract/intro.

The comparison to DQN/PPO/TRPO appears favorable only because these baselines are run on the same shaped rewards but seemingly without comparable hyperparameter tuning effort as given to ICR-RL (extensive epsilon-schedule, alpha, and context-size ablation only for ICR-RL); this raises concerns about fairness of the comparison and reproducibility of claimed competitiveness.

No statistical significance testing despite only 5–10 seeds, and performance differences between ICR-RL and DQN in Figure 2 are often within highly overlapping confidence bands (e.g., CartPole, MountainCar), making the central claim of 'competitiveness' weakly supported.

The theoretical justification for why TabPFN (trained purely on i.i.d., non-RL, non-bootstrapped synthetic data) functions well as a Q-function regressor under non-stationary, correlated, bootstrapped targets is hand-waved ('unexpected robustness') rather than rigorously analyzed; no convergence guarantees or formal treatment of the mismatch are provided, despite this being the central and most surprising claim of the paper.

Runtime/scalability is a serious unaddressed limitation: the quadratic attention complexity combined with full re-running of ICR-FQI (multiple forward passes over the entire context) on every new high-reward episode likely makes the method far more computationally expensive at inference than it appears; no wall-clock comparison to DQN/PPO/TRPO total training time is given, only relative context-engineering runtime (Figure 5).

The context-engineering experiments (Figure 3) lack clear experimental details (which environment, budget size B, number of seeds) and the described methods (ND, ED, RV, SC, L) are ad hoc heuristics without principled justification or theoretical backing; the claim that ND is 'best' is drawn from a single plot without statistical rigor.

The sparse-reward experiment with TabICL (Section 4.3, Figure 6) is a single, underspecified ablation with no detail on why TabICL outperforms TabPFN, undermining the paper's attempt to generalize claims about ICR backbones; it reads as an incomplete side observation rather than a controlled study.

Several claims in the abstract and conclusion ('can compete with,' 'matches or exceeds... established baselines such as DQN') are stronger than what the mixed, highly overlapping, environment-limited results actually support, particularly for Acrobot where DQN clearly and substantially outperforms ICR-RL.

Reproducibility concerns: central implementation details, such as how TabPFN's bucketed/discretized output heads are adapted for Q-value regression, how the context is structured for each FQI iteration computationally, and exact wall-clock costs, are only partially described; no code release is mentioned.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the approach largely combines an existing reduction (FQI from classical RL theory) with an existing pretrained model (TabPFN) in a relatively straightforward way; the main new contributions are engineering heuristics (context management) rather than fundamental methodological or theoretical advances.

strengths: The central idea—reducing RL to in-context regression via FQI and applying an off-the-shelf regression foundation model (TabPFN) with zero RL-specific training—is conceptually clean and interesting, offering a genuinely different path toward gradient-free RL foundation models compared to prior transformer-RL work (Decision Transformer, RL2, Algorithm Distillation, OmniRL) that all require RL-specific pretraining.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad for the claims made: three classic-control environments, comparisons against DQN/PPO/TRPO plus additional baselines (KNN-FQI, TabICL, TabFlex) in the appendix, multiple seeds, and an ablation study over key hyperparameters (percentile refit, context budget, exploration schedule, FQI iteration count).

The context-engineering contribution (Naive/Embedding De-duplication, Reward-Variance retention vs. naive recency/stale-context baselines) is a practical and seemingly novel addition that addresses a real scalability bottleneck for in-context RL methods, with evidence that it both improves performance and reduces runtime.

The discussion section honestly engages with the mismatch between TabPFN's i.i.d. pretraining assumptions and the non-stationary, correlated nature of RL data, and the limitations section is forthright about scalability, sparse-reward difficulties, and quadratic attention costs.
Implementation details (hyperparameters, reward-shaping functions, baseline configurations) are reported in detail in the appendix, supporting reproducibility of the reported experiments.
weaknesses: All evaluated environments are low-dimensional, discrete-action classic-control tasks (CartPole, MountainCar, Acrobot); despite claims in Table 1 that the method supports continuous state-action spaces, no continuous-action or higher-dimensional experiment is actually shown, so the significance/generality claims are not fully substantiated.

Reward shaping was applied to all environments for both ICR-RL and the baselines because the method reportedly fails under sparse rewards; since CartPole/MountainCar/Acrobot are normally solvable by DQN/PPO/TRPO without custom shaping, this raises fairness/validity concerns about whether the shaping functions were tuned in a way that differentially favors ICR-RL, and it undercuts the sparse-reward robustness of the proposed approach.

The core method is essentially nonparametric FQI with TabPFN substituted as the regressor; the conceptual novelty beyond "use a stronger nonparametric regressor for FQI" (as compared, e.g., to classical KNN-FQI, which is already discussed in related work) is somewhat incremental, and the paper does not clearly articulate why this specific reduction constitutes more than an engineering demonstration.

No wall-clock or compute-cost comparison is provided against the neural baselines despite the stated motivation of avoiding the computational/memory overhead of backpropagation; given that context size grows and attention is quadratic, it is unclear whether ICR-RL is actually cheaper in practice than small DQN/PPO networks on these simple tasks.

The finding that fewer FQI iterations (α≈0.1) outperform the theoretically prescribed near-convergence regime (α≈1) is noted as "surprising" but not analyzed or explained, leaving an important discrepancy between theory and the empirical procedure unresolved.

Scalability is explicitly flagged as untested for higher-dimensional or visual tasks, and given TabPFN's known context-size limitations, it is unclear how the approach would extend beyond small, low-dimensional control problems, which limits the practical significance of the "foundation model for RL" framing.

Statistical rigor is limited to shaded-variance plots across seeds; no significance tests or more rigorous statistical comparison (e.g., confidence intervals on final performance, sample-efficiency curves with formal tests) are reported to support claims of being "competitive" with or "outperforming" baselines.
